summary.value: Symptoms begin as small yellow or white slightly raised spots on leaf surfaces that enlarge into reddish-brown pustules (uredinia) about 1/8 inch or smaller; pustules may be surrounded by a yellow border and release rusty spores, and severe infection causes leaves to curl, dry, turn brown, and drop prematurely.

diagnostic_features.value: Rust can be distinguished from other foliar diseases because the rust-colored spores will rub off, while with other foliar diseases, nothing rubs off.

value: Rotate bean with non-host crops / rotate away from any bean for two years to remove sources of inoculum.
Plow under or bury infected crop residues and bean debris right after harvest.
Eliminate volunteer bean plants.
Plant within recommended planting periods (e.g. May 15 to June 15) to reduce late-season exposure to the pathogen.
Select planting dates and schedule irrigation to avoid long periods of leaf wetness when temperatures are warm (e.g. avoid foliage staying wet at night for more than 10 hours).
Plant rust-resistant cultivars (available for many market classes including pinto, great northern, small white, red kidney, and black beans), recognizing many races of the fungus exist.
Avoid over-application of nitrogen and ensure adequate potassium fertilization.
Disinfect poles used in pole-bean production.
Scout fields frequently during late vegetative to early pod development for initial rust pustules.

Apply protectant and/or systemic fungicides such as Maneb/Manex (30-day phi), Endura, Headline, Priaxor, or Vertisan (21-day phi), Bravo/Terranil, Folicur or Quadris (14-day phi), Proline (7-day phi), or Fontelis (0-day phi); consult Cooperative Extension or the latest New England Vegetable Management Guide for current chemical recommendations.
treatments.quote: Cultural practices such as crop rotation and burial of bean debris will remove potential sources of inoculum. Planting within recommended periods for this region (May 15 to June 15) will reduce late season exposure to high levels of the pathogen ... treatment with a labeled fungicide such as Maneb/Manex (30-day preharvest interval = phi), Endura, Headline, Priaxor, or Vertisan (21 day phi), Bravo/Terranil, Folicur or Quadris (14 day phi), Proline (7 day phi), or Fontelis (0 day phi) should be considered at the first confirmed signs of rust

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: The fungus that causes white mold, Sclerotinia sclerotiorum , is widely distributed in relatively cool and moist areas throughout the world .

type_of_disease.quote: The fungus, Sclerotinia sclerotiorum , causes white mold.

value: Foliar
Stem

Whole plant
affected_parts.quote: The first symptom is usually water-soaked lesions on stem and pods. The fungus may invade the stem near the soil line, causing a rapid wilting and death of the entire plant, or it may invade pods or branches and foliage that comes in contact with colonized tissue.

summary.value: White mold first appears as pale, often bleached, water-soaked (watery) rot lesions on stems, leaves, and pods; white threadlike, cottony mycelium is often visible on rotted tissue under moist conditions, after which affected tissue dries and bleaches to a pale tan, beige, or almost white color and black sclerotia develop.
summary.quote: White mold first appears as a watery rot on stems, leaves, and pods. White mycelium (threadlike hyphae) is often visible on the surface of rotted tissue under moist conditions.

diagnostic_features.value: The development of black, irregularly shaped (round to oblong) sclerotiaâ€”compact masses of myceliaâ€”within the white cottony fungal growth is the best diagnostic feature; sclerotia are white early in development and turn black when fully developed, formed on plant surfaces and inside pods or stems, while affected tissue dries quickly and bleaches to a pale tan, beige, or almost white color.
diagnostic_features.quote: The development of black, irregularly shaped sclerotia (compact masses of mycelia) is the best diagnostic feature.

value: Phytophthora blight

look_alikes.quote: White mold on pepper can be distinguished from Phytophthora blight, which also affects stems, by presence of white cottony fungal growth and sclerotia, additionally, with Phytophthora blight affected stems are darker brown and usually there are also symptoms on leaves and fruit plus the growing tip may be blighted.

value: Rotate with non-host crops (small grains, corn, rye, wheat, grasses, cereals) for at least 2-3 years, and up to 3-8 years, to reduce soil inoculum and sclerotia populations.
Use wide row spacing (36 inches recommended) to increase air movement and promote drying of the soil and plant canopy.
Use management practices that reduce heavy canopies and increase air movement.
Avoid heavy applications of nitrogen / over-fertilization, which can produce excessive, dense, lush canopies.

Plant erect, upright, open-canopy (open-base) varieties that hold pods off the ground and do not produce excessive foliage near ground level; resistant bean varieties (including dry bean types) are available.
Orient bean rows in the direction of the prevailing winds to promote air drainage and drying of plant and soil surfaces.
Avoid planting the most susceptible crops in fields surrounded by dense woods that restrict air circulation.
Time irrigations to allow drying of the plant canopy before nightfall and avoid excessive irrigation after petal fall.
Plant garbanzo beans later (December through early February) rather than early (early November) to avoid heavy canopies that increase humidity.
Scout and inspect plants for symptoms beginning at emergence/bloom, keeping written notes and photographic records of occurrence and severity.
Practice good weed control, removing susceptible weeds (in particular ragweed) from the field.
Avoid wounds and remove affected plants.
Incorporate debris promptly after harvest and use deep plowing to bury sclerotia and reduce sclerotia production.
Field flooding during warm temperatures destroys sclerotia.
Use a timely harvest with rapid cooling and pod storage at 45Â°F to 50Â°F for effective postharvest control.

Apply foliar fungicides starting at early bloom (1% to 10% bloom) in fields with a history of white mold, obtaining thorough coverage with high water volume (50 gallons per acre minimum) and high pressure (100 to 200 psi).
Conventional fungicides in FRAC groups 1, 2, 3, 7, 11, 12 and 29 are labeled for white mold, in addition to contact fungicides copper and chlorothalonil.
BOSCALID (Endura) at 8 to 11 oz/A at the beginning of flowering and again at full bloom.
THIOPHANATE METHYL (Topsin M WSB at 1 to 1.5 lb/A; T-Methyl 4.5F AG / Topsin 4.5 FL at 30 to 40 fl oz/A).
Blocker 4F (Group 14) at 4 pints/A at planting and again on 2- to 3-week intervals when disease is severe.
Botran 75W (Group 14) at 2 2/3 lb/A on 7-day intervals.
Cannonball WG (Group 12) at 7 oz/A when 10% of plants have at least one open blossom.
Fontelis at 16 to 30 fl oz/A at the beginning of flowering and again at full bloom.
Luna Privilege at 6.84 fl oz/A on 14-day intervals.
Rovral 4 Flowable at 1.5 to 2 pints/A when 10% of plants have at least one open bloom.
Omega 500F (Group 29) at 0.5 to 0.85 pint/A when 10% to 30% of plants have at least one open blossom.
Switch 62.5WG (Group 12 + 9) at 11 to 14 oz/A.
Jet-Ag at 0.75 to 3.9 fl oz/5 gal water as a weekly preventative treatment.
Biological/soil treatments: Contans WG (a parasitic fungus that attacks sclerotia) at 1 to 4 lb/A as a preplant or postharvest treatment.
Regalia Biofungicide (Group P5) at 1 to 4 quarts/A on 7- to 10-day intervals.
Double Nickel LC at 1 to 6 quarts/A at planting and again at cultivation.
Serenade Opti at 14 to 20 oz/A on 7- to 10-day intervals.
Stargus at 2 to 4 quarts/A plus a nonionic surfactant on 7- to 10-day intervals.
treatments.quote: Cultural control Reduce humidity and high-moisture periods within the plant canopy and field. ... Chemical control In fields with a history of white mold, apply fungicide at 1% to 10% bloom ... Biological control Contans WG at 1 to 4 lb/A
